title: Kohlrausch's Law and Molar Conductivity

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Electrochemistry

expression: Λm = κ/C  ;  Λm°(weak electrolyte) = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋  (Kohlrausch's law of independent migration)
explanation: Molar conductivity Λm is specific conductance κ divided by molar concentration C; it increases with dilution for all electrolytes, but a directly measurable limiting value Λm° (at infinite dilution) can only be found by extrapolation for STRONG electrolytes. For WEAK electrolytes, Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions is used instead: at infinite dilution, each ion migrates independently and contributes a fixed value regardless of its accompanying ion, so Λm° for a weak electrolyte can be calculated by combining known Λm° values of strong electrolytes containing the same ions.

variables.meaning: Limiting molar conductivity of the cation and anion
Number of cations/anions produced per formula unit

workedExample.scenario: Find Λm°(CH₃COOH) using Λm°(HCl), Λm°(CH₃COONa), and Λm°(NaCl) via Kohlrausch's law.
workedExample.result: This combination cancels out the common Na⁺ and Cl⁻ contributions, leaving just CH₃COO⁻ and H⁺ combined

commonMistakes: Trying to find Λm° for a weak electrolyte by direct extrapolation of a Λm vs √C plot — weak electrolytes don't give a straight, easily-extrapolated line near infinite dilution (unlike strong electrolytes), so Kohlrausch's law combination method must be used instead.
Forgetting to account for the number of ions (ν₊, ν₋) produced per formula unit when combining values, especially for salts with unequal ion counts.
genZNote: Weak electrolytes can't extrapolate their way to Λm° — Kohlrausch's law does the math trick instead.
